short: China's Cyberspace Administration publishes every generative AI service cleared for public release. The counts, the two-tier split, and what they mean.
title: China's Generative AI Filing Registry
subtitle: What the CAC publishes, and what the numbers show
body_html:
On this page

  • The one thing no other country publishes
  • The numbers
  • Filed and registered are not the same
  • What it requires of a provider
  • What the growth shows
  • What this does not tell you
  • Primary sources

The one-paragraph answer

A generative AI service offered to the public in China must be filed with the Cyberspace Administration of China before release, and the CAC publishes the list. As of 30 June 2026 the published cumulative total was 988 filed services and 598 registered applications. The announcements are issued roughly every two months under the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, and each states the new count for the period and the running total. No other jurisdiction publishes a comparable register.

The one thing no other country publishes

Every jurisdiction covered on this site regulates AI in some form. Only one publishes a list of the individual services it has cleared.

The EU AI Act creates obligations and conformity assessments but no public register of approved systems. US federal and state law imposes duties on deployers without licensing the models. China's filing regime is different in kind: a generative AI service with public opinion attributes or social mobilisation capability goes through a filing procedure before it reaches users, and the resulting list is published with model names and filing numbers.

That makes it the only place where the question "how many generative AI services are actually in public service in this country" has a published answer rather than an estimate.

The numbers

Each CAC announcement states the new count for the period and the cumulative total. Read down the right-hand column for the shape of it.

The 446 figure for 2025 is the whole year, not a two-month period, and is shown here as the CAC stated it rather than reshaped to fit the rows around it.

A later announcement covering July and August 2026 is reported to add 124 filings and bring the cumulative total past 1,100. We have not confirmed that one against cac.gov.cn and it is therefore not in the table. Every row above traces to an announcement on the CAC's own site.

Filed and registered are not the same

The two columns count different things, and conflating them overstates the number of distinct AI systems in China by more than half.

Filing is completed with the national CAC and applies to a service that provides model capability itself. Registration is handled by provincial internet authorities and applies to an application or feature that calls an already-filed model through an API or by other means. An app built on a filed model registers; it does not file.

So 988 filed and 598 registered is not 1,586 AI systems. It is 988 model services, plus 598 downstream products that use them and are logged separately. The distinction matters commercially: it decides whether a company carries the regulatory burden itself or relies on an approved supplier.

There is a visible obligation attached. A live application or feature must display, prominently or on its product detail page, which filed or registered service it uses, naming the model and its filing or registration number.

What it requires of a provider

The regime rests on the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, which the announcements cite as their authority. The practical shape for a provider:

  • A service with public opinion attributes or social mobilisation capability must complete filing or registration before it is offered publicly.
  • Filing goes to the national body; registration for a downstream application goes through the local authority where the company sits.
  • The filing number, once issued, is a public identifier and must be displayed by the products that rely on it.
  • The list is published and updated, so a provider's presence or absence from it is externally checkable.

What the growth shows

Two things are visible in the numbers that are not in any announcement.

The rate is not steady. Filings ran at 48 in the first two months of 2026, then 72, then 120. The May to June period added more filed services than the previous four months together. Whatever is driving that, it is not a regulator slowing approvals down.

Registrations are growing faster in proportion. In August 2025 registered applications were 49% of filed services. By June 2026 they were 61%. More of the ecosystem is being built on top of already-approved models rather than filing new ones, which is what a maturing platform market looks like.

What this does not tell you

Three limits worth stating, because a published register invites more confidence than it can carry.

It is a count of services cleared for public offering, not of models developed. Research systems, internal tools and anything without public opinion attributes are outside it.

It says nothing about scale. A filing number is the same whether the service has ten users or a hundred million.

And the announcements publish counts and lists, not the assessments behind them. What a filing required, what was refused and why are not disclosed, so the register tells you what passed and nothing about the bar.

Primary sources

Announcements from the Cyberspace Administration of China. Where a compliance decision turns on exact wording, read the source rather than this page.
